about: What this plugin is known not to hold. A limit written only in prose is lost the next time someone reads past it, so every one of them has a row here and the row is checked. `where` names the records that state it: `dNNNN` a decision record, `spec` the specification, `handoff` the handoff page, `escapes` the escapes ledger, `trials` the trial protocol. `plan` is the disposition the owner locked on 2026-11-13; a row never silently changes plan. Closed rows stay, so that a claim can be checked against what closed it.

areas.guide: The skill that walks a person through the layers of a new design system.
areas.adopt: The skill that records what a repository already has, without changing it.
areas.audit: The read-only report on how far a repository has got.
areas.checks: The gate tool and the browser test it installs.
areas.rules: The page a screen-building agent reads before it starts.
areas.specimen: The sheet that draws the options on the repository's own screen.
areas.book: The handoff book drawn from the repository.
areas.reference-app: The example application this repository carries as its proof.
areas.trials: The runs by independent agents that test the plugin.

kinds.partial-check: A check holds less than the ledger row it proves claims.
kinds.no-check: A rule is written down and nothing holds it.
kinds.wrong-signal: A report or a check can mislead the person reading it.
kinds.stack-bound: It works only on one kind of repository.
kinds.unproven: It is built, but nothing independent has exercised it.
kinds.conflict: Another document in the system tells a builder the opposite.

plans.fix: Meant to be closed by this project; the roadmap says when.
plans.keep: Accepted as it is, stated here so nobody counts on more.
plans.hand-off: The fix belongs to another repository, named in `repo`.

limits.note: The contrast check covers two pairs of the primary colour only, while the audit counts the row as fully held by the machine.
Nothing measures the contrast of a hover or pointer state; the one real failure was caught by accident.
Target size is read as a height from source classes only, so a control narrower than the threshold still passes.
For column width and table density the machine holds only that no screen overrides them, yet the audit counts both rows as held.
Nothing forces a screen with an action done at once to declare a failure state, so a screen that swallows the error passes.
The focus check only asks that something holds focus, so focus landing on the wrong thing passes.
An adopted brand colour is not pinned, so swapping it for another colour that also meets contrast passes.
For rows pointing at a repository's own lint rule or test, that the check can go red is inferred from its shape, never tried.
The browser check for a row's actions reads the first row of the first table only.
In an adopted repository the colour checks only go red once the token command is run again, so the gate can be green on stale values.
A row pointing at a repository's own tagged test stays self-declared: this plugin's tool never runs that test.
Nothing can make a person write a line in the escapes ledger, so the governance tier passes on an empty file.
Deleting the note that says nobody confirmed a row turns nothing red, and a changed blueprint answer always reds under the name of the palette row.
The rule that a focused heading shows a ring has no check and lives on the rules page only.
A colour written as a blend of two others is never read, so the dark mode of a repository that writes them has no check at all.
In an existing repository adopt says nothing about screen kinds, screen sizes, import direction or the escapes ledger.
Adopt has never been run for real in any repository but this one; elsewhere it has only ever been previewed.
The audit reads only a web repository that writes its values as CSS variables, and a tool pointer needs a Makefile or an npm script.
After a successful adopt the audit's next step still points back at adopt, even when running it again would add nothing.
Pictures can only be drawn in a repository built with Vite that carries the floor's test browser; elsewhere the sheet and the book fall back to words.

While the sheet is open the frame header is reachable by mouse but by keyboard and screen reader only once it closes, and its position is measured when the sheet opens and never again if the window changes size.
The rule for moving between screens has no reference implementation, so it is unproven in code.
limits.closed_by: the frame in src/App.tsx, built together with the second screen of the list kind

limits.note: A font size or spacing unit declared inside the framework's theme block cannot be read, so adopt neither reports nor records it.
The token file carries colour, corner radius and type only: there is nothing for font, spacing, elevation or motion.
The component reader matches the floor's way of writing components rather than parsing them, so a component written another way is listed without its variants.
The component register carries no states, props, parts or level, and never reads components outside the library folder.
A control that declares no height of its own is not measured at all, and appears in the register as a control with no height.
Turning a class into pixels assumes the framework's four-pixel unit, so a repository that declares another unit gets wrong numbers.
A column's width is counted in digit widths, so a text column is only approximately right, and the starting sample lengths are a machine proposal.
No rule says how each column type is formatted, edited in place or filtered, and a number printed without the formatter is caught by nothing.
The states row holds that a screen declares its states, not that it draws them.
The check for words written into a screen misses text built by joining strings, and alignment set on an element nested inside a cell still slips through.
An error message is recognised only through the floor's alert component, so a repository that reports errors any other way gets no row.
The states row depends on the floor's list of screens, so a repository without that file gets no states row.
The notification row holds only that no screen goes around the repository's own module; which message belongs on which channel is a person's review.
Four rules for what follows an action live on the rules page with no check: the list changing in place, undo, the empty state, and moving between screens.
Import direction holds only where a screen-kind page exists, does not follow an import through a package, and lets two files inside one part import each other.
Three rules have no check: at most two buttons on a row, each row waiting on its own, and the ledger being only for shared rules.
The narrow-width check measures the sample data only: a name longer than about twenty-two characters would turn it red, and no state carries one.
Only the head of a screen-kind page is read; the order of information and the prose in its body are checked by nobody.
A screen that builds its own overlay or a separate record page is caught by nothing, and a record opened while the list still loads does not take focus.
The table of evidence a repository may already have recognises the floor's lint rules only, so a repository with its own must write those rows by hand.
Adopt installs the value checks only where the repository's gate collects the included make files; another shape of gate gets self-declared rows.
The threshold that decides a repository has a brand colour of its own is a machine guess, so a tinted grey can be overwritten.
A ledger row records no confidence in its check, and has no pointer kind for a data type, another linter, or the acceptance kit's own grading.
Which layer each standard decision belongs to is a machine judgement nobody has challenged; four edge cases carry a note instead.
The audit cannot tell a decision nobody has made from one made somewhere its ledger does not record.
The sheet can only show what the reference implementation happens to use, and the swatches and size list that make up for it are drawings from values, not real components.
Pictures are not the same to the pixel across machines; only the list of options, their values and the page itself are.
Whether the book looks good can only be judged by a person, and three of its eight sheets have never been looked at.
The book's list of what it shows leaves out the pictures and the words on screens, so a stale picture still reads as matching.
Fonts are not carried in the book, four components that need a parent are not drawn at all, and two others are drawn bare.
What the page for the list kind of screen says is a machine proposal the owner has not confirmed.
Whatever was fixed after the most recent trial has not been tried by an independent agent, which is true by construction after every trial.
An independent agent cannot look at a sheet on a person's behalf, so the parts chosen by eye have no agent-run acceptance.
The test that builds an empty repository borrows this repository's real stylesheet and Makefile, and the full gate only ever runs here.
There is a continuous-integration file but no remote, so every check has only ever run on one machine.
The token measurement this project promised has never been run, and the earlier claim that the plugin saves tokens was withdrawn as unfounded.
The independent critique's largest risk, that this is a reskin of a component library that already supplies values and components, has never been answered.
The plugin does not touch rework caused by tests or infrastructure, and cannot say whether the experience it produces is any good.
The wording of the guide's questions is policed by a list of words to avoid, not by requiring every term to be in the vocabulary.
This repository has declared nothing to the acceptance kit, so the kit's own tier has not moved although both artifacts exist.
The repository's guide for agents does not mention the plugin folder, because that file belongs to the tool that laid the repository.
The language and the currency of the example application were inferred by machine and nobody has confirmed them.
Nothing fails when a trial is run and no row is added to the series, so the numbers depend on the session remembering.
The standard brief runs against a repository that keeps growing, so two runs of it are not strictly the same task.
The floor's three browser tests carry no decision tag, so no ledger row can point at them and the accessibility check runs twice here.

Floor documents tell a builder the opposite of approved rules on column width, on locking a button, on a link dressed as a button, on installing a component, and on the widths the browser checks run at.
Colours written in the perceptual notation slip past the acceptance kit's comparison of raw colours against tokens, which reads hexadecimal only.
